# Portugal vs Florida

Portuguese law is never used to answer a Florida exam question. Each entry states whether its Portuguese side was verified.

## PT-01 · Who must hold the license

**Portuguese context.** Under Lei n.º 15/2013, carrying on real estate mediation as a business requires a license from IMPIC, I.P. The license is held by the mediation business (a company or an individual entrepreneur). Consultants who work inside a licensed agency usually operate under the agency's license.

**Florida context.** Every individual who performs a real estate service for another for compensation must personally hold a Florida license (sales associate or broker), unless an exemption in s. 475.011 applies. A sales associate's license is only usable while registered under one employing broker.

**The important difference.** Florida licenses the person, not only the firm. A consultant who would work under an agency's license in Portugal needs their own license in Florida, and it is inactive until a broker employs them.

**Practical example.** Ana moves from a Lisbon agency to Miami. In Lisbon she showed homes under her agency's AMI license. In Miami she may not show a listing for a commission until she has passed the exam, been issued a license and been registered with a broker.

**Examination implication.** Any answer that lets an unlicensed employee earn per-deal pay for showing, negotiating or listing is wrong. Unlicensed practice is a third-degree felony.

**Memory aid.** Portugal licenses the agency; Florida licenses each person.

**Practice question.** A licensed Florida brokerage hires an unlicensed assistant and pays $150 for every buyer she shows a home to. Lawful?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

No. Showing property for compensation per transaction is a real estate service for another for compensation; she needs a license. A salary for clerical work only would be lawful.

</details>

*Portuguese side: Partly verified: IMPIC licensing requirement for individual or corporate providers (impic.pt; Lei 15/2013). How consultants inside agencies operate: requires verification..* Lessons: L01-1, L02-1

## PT-02 · The regulator

**Portuguese context.** IMPIC, I.P. (Instituto dos Mercados Públicos, do Imobiliário e da Construção) licenses and supervises mediation businesses and approves standard mediation contract models.

**Florida context.** Two bodies share the work. The Florida Real Estate Commission (FREC, 7 members) makes rules (Chapter 61J2, F.A.C.) and disciplines licensees. The Department of Business and Professional Regulation (DBPR) processes applications, issues licenses and investigates complaints. Courts handle crimes and civil damages.

**The important difference.** Florida splits rulemaking/discipline (FREC) from administration/investigation (DBPR). Exam questions test which body does what.

**Practical example.** A buyer complains that a sales associate kept part of a deposit. DBPR investigates; a FREC probable-cause panel decides whether to proceed; FREC issues the final order; only a court can order jail or damages.

**Examination implication.** 'Which body investigates?' → DBPR. 'Which body suspends or revokes?' → FREC. 'Which body imprisons?' → a court.

**Memory aid.** DBPR digs, FREC decides, courts jail.

**Practice question.** Who issues a Florida real estate license, and who may revoke it?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

The DBPR issues it; the FREC may revoke it (after due process).

</details>

*Portuguese side: verified: impic.pt (licensing, model contracts).* Lessons: L01-1, L03-1

## PT-03 · Entry requirements: education and exam

**Portuguese context.** IMPIC's listed requirements for a mediation license are commercial good standing (idoneidade comercial) and civil liability insurance (or equivalent guarantee), plus fees. No state exam or minimum course hours appear in the requirements.

**Florida context.** Sales associate: 63-hour course, state exam (75/100), fingerprints and background check, then 45 hours of post-license education before the first renewal and 14 hours of CE every 2 years after.

**The important difference.** Florida has a full education-and-exam pathway with deadlines that can void the license. Portugal's entry test is good standing and insurance.

**Practical example.** A Portuguese agency owner with 15 years' experience still has to complete the 63-hour Florida course and pass the exam; experience abroad does not replace it (mutual recognition covers only certain US states).

**Examination implication.** Know 63 / 45 / 14 and which deadline voids (post-license) versus which inactivates (CE).

**Memory aid.** 63 to enter, 45 to stay, 14 to keep.

**Practice question.** A licensee misses the 45-hour post-license course before the first renewal. Result?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

The license becomes null and void; to practice again they must requalify from the 63-hour course and exam.

</details>

*Portuguese side: verified: impic.pt licensing requirements page.* Lessons: L02-3, L03-3

## PT-04 · Representing both sides

**Portuguese context.** In Portuguese practice an agency often deals with both seller and buyer in the same sale while the mediation contract is signed with one client. The exact statutory duties toward the non-client party require verification.

**Florida context.** Florida allows three relationships: single agent, transaction broker (presumed by default), or no brokerage relationship. A brokerage may NOT be a single agent for both buyer and seller in the same transaction (dual agency is illegal). The lawful way to work both sides is as a transaction broker to both.

**The important difference.** Florida names and defines the relationship and its duties by statute (3/7/9 duties). 'Representing both sides' as a fiduciary is unlawful.

**Practical example.** Your brokerage lists a condo as single agent for the seller. Your own buyer client wants it. Before continuing, the seller must sign a Consent to Transition to Transaction Broker; you then act as transaction broker for both.

**Examination implication.** Any answer choice with 'dual agent' is wrong. 'Unless otherwise established in writing, a licensee is presumed to be a transaction broker.'

**Memory aid.** Florida: no dual agency — transition to transaction broker.

**Practice question.** A Florida broker acts as single agent for a seller and wants to work with a buyer on the same property. What is required?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

The seller's written consent to transition to transaction broker before the change; the broker then acts as transaction broker for both parties.

</details>

*Portuguese side: requires verification.* Lessons: L04-1, L04-2

## PT-05 · Listing / mediation contract form

**Portuguese context.** The contrato de mediação imobiliária must be in writing; missing mandatory content makes it null, and the mediation company cannot invoke that nullity. Mediation contract models with general clauses need IMPIC approval or must follow the official model (Portaria n.º 228/2018).

**Florida context.** A listing agreement is an employment contract between seller and BROKERAGE. Florida written listings must have a definite expiration date, may not renew automatically, and a copy must be given to the person signing within 24 hours. Listing types: open, exclusive agency, exclusive right of sale (and net).

**The important difference.** Florida's rules focus on expiration, no auto-renewal, the 24-hour copy, and the commission consequences of the listing type.

**Practical example.** A seller signs an exclusive-agency listing with your brokerage and then sells to her neighbour without help. No commission is due. Under an exclusive-right-of-sale listing it would be.

**Examination implication.** Know which listing type pays when the owner finds the buyer: exclusive right of sale → yes; exclusive agency → no; open → only the procuring broker.

**Memory aid.** RIGHT of sale = paid regardless. AGENCY = owner keeps the right to sell free.

**Practice question.** Which three requirements apply to every written listing in Florida?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

A definite expiration date; no automatic renewal clause; a copy delivered to the person signing within 24 hours.

</details>

*Portuguese side: verified: Lei 15/2013 art. 16 (written form, nullity, model approval) via diariodarepublica.pt / impic.pt.* Lessons: L11-3

## PT-06 · When the commission is earned

**Portuguese context.** Remuneration is due on the conclusion and perfection of the deal the mediation aimed at; under exclusivity it remains due if the deal fails for reasons attributable to the client (Lei 15/2013, art. 19). Courts require a causal link between the mediator's activity and the deal.

**Florida context.** Commission terms come from the listing contract. Under exclusive right of sale the brokerage earns the fee whoever sells; under an open listing only the procuring cause earns it. A sales associate may be paid only by their employing broker.

**The important difference.** In Florida the payment path is fixed by law: seller → brokerage → associate. An associate can never accept payment directly from a customer.

**Practical example.** A grateful seller hands the sales associate a $500 gift card at closing. That is a violation unless it goes through the broker.

**Examination implication.** 'Associate accepted payment from the seller/another broker' → violation. Commission rates are negotiable; a 'standard rate' suggests price fixing.

**Memory aid.** Money flows through the broker.

**Practice question.** May a Florida sales associate sue the buyer directly for an unpaid commission?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

No. The associate's claim is against the employing broker; only the broker can sue the party who owes the brokerage fee.

</details>

*Portuguese side: verified: Lei 15/2013 art. 19; STJ 2019 decision on causal link (diariodarepublica.pt).* Lessons: L11-3, L05-4

## PT-07 · Deposits and earnest money

**Portuguese context.** A deposit paid on a contrato-promessa is presumed to be 'sinal'. Under Código Civil art. 442: if the payer defaults, the other party keeps it; if the recipient defaults, the payer can demand double. Who holds the money in practice requires verification.

**Florida context.** Earnest money (binder) is normally held in ESCROW by the broker, a title company or an attorney. Strict clocks apply: associate to broker by end of next business day; broker deposits by end of the third business day. On a dispute the broker follows the conflicting-demand procedures. Contracts often treat the deposit as liquidated damages if the buyer defaults.

**The important difference.** There is no automatic 'return double' rule in Florida exam content. The focus is on escrow handling and deadlines.

**Practical example.** Buyer gives your associate a $20,000 check on Friday. Associate must deliver it to the broker by end of Monday; broker must deposit it by end of Wednesday (no holidays).

**Examination implication.** Count BUSINESS days. Do not apply the double-deposit rule.

**Memory aid.** Sinal doubles in Portugal; escrow clocks run in Florida.

**Practice question.** The buyer defaults on a Florida contract. Does the seller receive double the deposit?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

No. The seller's remedy depends on the contract (often the deposit as liquidated damages). The broker releases escrowed funds only per the contract, written agreement, or a settlement procedure.

</details>

*Portuguese side: verified: Código Civil art. 442 (diariodarepublica.pt).* Lessons: L05-1, L05-2, L11-2

## PT-08 · Two-step (CPCV + escritura) vs one contract and a closing

**Portuguese context.** Typically a contrato-promessa de compra e venda (CPCV) is signed, then the final sale is formalized by escritura pública or documento particular autenticado and registered. Details require verification.

**Florida context.** Buyer and seller sign one contract for sale and purchase (usually the FR/BAR form). The buyer gets equitable title. At closing the seller delivers a deed, which is then recorded.

**The important difference.** The Florida sale contract is itself the binding purchase agreement. No second 'promise' document exists, and a notary is not what makes the deed valid.

**Practical example.** After both parties initial the final counteroffer, the effective date starts the inspection and financing deadlines. 'Time is of the essence' makes each deadline strict.

**Examination implication.** Buyer under contract holds equitable title; legal title passes at closing by delivery and acceptance of the deed.

**Memory aid.** Contract → equitable title. Deed delivered → legal title.

**Practice question.** What does a buyer hold between contract and closing?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

Equitable title.

</details>

*Portuguese side: requires verification.* Lessons: L11-2, L11-4

## PT-09 · Transfer taxes

**Portuguese context.** The buyer pays IMT (progressive, on the higher of price and taxable property value) and Imposto do Selo at 0.8%. Young buyers up to 35 have exemptions up to set limits (330,539 € in 2026 tables for full exemption). Decreto-Lei n.º 97/2026 sets a 7.5% IMT rate for non-residents buying housing, with exceptions.

**Florida context.** Documentary stamp tax on the DEED: $0.70 per $100 (Miami-Dade single-family $0.60), customarily the SELLER's cost. Note stamps ($0.35 per $100) and intangible tax (2 mills on new mortgages) are the buyer's costs when financing.

**The important difference.** Florida's main transfer tax on the deed is customarily the seller's. Florida's rates are flat per $100 and rounded UP to the next $100, with no progressive brackets.

**Practical example.** $350,050 sale in Orange County: round up to $350,100 → 3,501 × $0.70 = $2,450.70 deed stamps, normally charged to the seller.

**Examination implication.** Round up to the next $100 for stamps. Intangible tax only on NEW money.

**Memory aid.** Seller pays 70 on the deed; buyer pays 35 + 2 mills on the loan.

**Practice question.** Who customarily pays deed stamps in Florida, and on what amount?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

The seller, on the full purchase price (including any mortgage assumed), at $0.70 per $100 or portion.

</details>

*Portuguese side: verified: Portal das Finanças (IMT tables 2026, IS 0.8%); Decreto-Lei 97/2026.* Lessons: L14-6

## PT-10 · Annual property tax

**Portuguese context.** IMI is an annual municipal tax on the registered taxable value (VPT). Rates and exemptions require verification.

**Florida context.** Ad valorem tax: the county property appraiser sets just value as of January 1; taxing authorities set millage. Homestead owners get exemptions ($25,000 + up to $25,000 non-school) and the Save Our Homes cap (3% or CPI). Bills mail November 1 with discounts; delinquent April 1.

**The important difference.** Florida taxes are computed in mills on taxable value after exemptions, and school vs non-school values can differ.

**Practical example.** Assessed $300,000, homestead: school taxable $275,000; non-school taxable $250,000 (using round $25,000 figures).

**Examination implication.** 1 mill = $1 per $1,000. Run school and non-school separately when exemptions differ.

**Memory aid.** Mills × taxable ÷ 1,000.

**Practice question.** Why can a homestead's school taxable value be higher than its non-school taxable value?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

The additional homestead exemption applies only to non-school levies.

</details>

*Portuguese side: requires verification.* Lessons: L18-1, L18-2

## PT-11 · Proving ownership: registry vs title insurance

**Portuguese context.** Ownership and charges are recorded in the land registry (registo predial). The degree of protection the registry gives a buyer requires verification.

**Florida context.** Documents are recorded in county public records, which give constructive notice. Buyers prove marketable title with an abstract plus attorney's opinion or, usually, title insurance (owner's policy for the price; lender's policy for the loan).

**The important difference.** Title insurance is a central product in Florida; the exam tests owner's vs lender's policy and what is covered (past defects, not future ones).

**Practical example.** A forged deed from 2015 surfaces after closing. The owner's title policy covers the loss; a lien the new owner creates in 2027 is not covered.

**Examination implication.** Recording protects against third parties; it is not required for a deed to be valid.

**Memory aid.** Record to warn the world; insure against the past.

**Practice question.** Is recording required for a Florida deed to be valid between grantor and grantee?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

No. Delivery and acceptance make it valid; recording gives constructive notice to the world.

</details>

*Portuguese side: requires verification.* Lessons: L09-3

## PT-12 · Deeds and warranties

**Portuguese context.** The sale is formalized in a public deed or authenticated private document. Portuguese practice does not use graded 'warranty deed' types (requires verification).

**Florida context.** Deed types are ranked by the warranties the grantor gives: general warranty (all time), special warranty (grantor's ownership period), bargain and sale (implied ownership, no warranties), quitclaim (no warranties). A valid Florida deed needs the grantor's signature before two witnesses and delivery/acceptance.

**The important difference.** Florida deeds carry warranty levels; two witnesses are a validity requirement for deeds.

**Practical example.** To clear an ex-spouse's possible interest from title, the ex-spouse signs a quitclaim deed.

**Examination implication.** Grantee does not sign. Notary acknowledgment is for recording.

**Memory aid.** General > special > bargain & sale > quitclaim.

**Practice question.** Which deed best cures a cloud on title?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

A quitclaim deed.

</details>

*Portuguese side: requires verification.* Lessons: L09-2

## PT-13 · Co-ownership and married couples

**Portuguese context.** Co-ownership (compropriedade) and the spouses' property regime (e.g., comunhão de adquiridos) govern shared ownership. Details require verification.

**Florida context.** Florida is NOT a community-property state. Co-owners hold as tenants in common (default for unmarried co-owners), joint tenants with right of survivorship (needs express language), or tenants by the entireties (married couples; presumed for a deed to spouses).

**The important difference.** Survivorship and creditor protection depend on the deed form and marital status, not on a marital property regime.

**Practical example.** Two unmarried friends buy a duplex with a deed that says nothing about survivorship. One dies; her share goes to her heirs, not to the friend.

**Examination implication.** Married + silent deed → entireties. Unmarried + silent → tenancy in common.

**Memory aid.** Married = entireties; strangers = in common.

**Practice question.** A married couple takes title 'John and Mary Smith, husband and wife'. John dies. Who owns the property?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

Mary, automatically, by survivorship under tenancy by the entireties.

</details>

*Portuguese side: requires verification.* Lessons: L08-3

## PT-14 · Condominium vs propriedade horizontal; cooperatives

**Portuguese context.** Apartment buildings are commonly divided under propriedade horizontal (fractions with common parts). Requires verification.

**Florida context.** A condominium is created by recording a declaration; the owner holds the unit in fee simple plus an undivided share of common elements (real property). A cooperative is different: a corporation owns the building and the buyer holds shares plus a proprietary lease, which is personal property.

**The important difference.** The cooperative form, where the buyer owns shares and not real estate, is unfamiliar to a Portuguese professional and is tested.

**Practical example.** A buyer of a Miami Beach co-op unit gets a stock certificate and a proprietary lease, and the board must approve the sale.

**Examination implication.** Co-op = personal property. Condo developer sale: 15-day cancellation.

**Memory aid.** Condo = deed; co-op = shares + lease.

**Practice question.** Which buyer owns real property: the condo buyer or the co-op buyer?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

The condo buyer.

</details>

*Portuguese side: requires verification.* Lessons: L08-5

## PT-15 · Life estate vs usufruto

**Portuguese context.** Usufruto gives the right to use and enjoy property belonging to another for a period, often for life. Requires verification.

**Florida context.** A life estate is an ownership estate measured by a life. The life tenant may use, lease or sell the life interest, must pay taxes and avoid waste; at death the property passes by remainder (to a third party) or reversion (back to the grantor or heirs).

**The important difference.** Florida vocabulary: life tenant, remainderman, reversion, waste, 'pur autre vie' (measured by another person's life).

**Practical example.** Mother deeds her home to her son but keeps a life estate. She may live there or lease it; when she dies the son (remainderman) owns it outright.

**Examination implication.** If the property returns to the grantor it is a reversion; to someone else, a remainder.

**Memory aid.** Remainder goes forward; reversion comes back.

**Practice question.** A life tenant leases the property for 10 years and dies after 2. What happens to the lease?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

It ends at the life tenant's death; the life tenant could only convey what she had.

</details>

*Portuguese side: requires verification.* Lessons: L08-1

## PT-16 · Family home protection

**Portuguese context.** Disposing of the family home (casa de morada de família) generally needs both spouses' consent. Requires verification.

**Florida context.** Florida homestead has three separate meanings: (1) protection from forced sale by most creditors (1/2 acre in a city, 160 acres outside); (2) restrictions on devise when a spouse or minor child survives, and the spouse must join in deeds and mortgages; (3) a property-tax exemption.

**The important difference.** Creditor protection is unusually strong in Florida but does not stop property taxes, the home's own mortgage, or construction liens for work on the home.

**Practical example.** A judgment creditor of a Tampa homeowner cannot force the sale of the 0.3-acre homestead; the bank holding the mortgage on that same home can foreclose.

**Examination implication.** Keep creditor protection separate from the tax exemption.

**Memory aid.** Homestead: shield, family lock, tax break — three different rules.

**Practice question.** Which creditor can force the sale of a Florida homestead: a credit-card judgment creditor or the county for unpaid property taxes?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

The county for unpaid property taxes.

</details>

*Portuguese side: requires verification.* Lessons: L08-4

## PT-17 · Units of measurement

**Portuguese context.** Metric system: m², hectares (1 ha = 10,000 m²).

**Florida context.** US customary units: feet, square feet, acres (43,560 sq ft), miles (5,280 ft), square yards (9 sq ft). Exam math never uses metric.

**The important difference.** Convert your intuition: 1 acre ≈ 4,047 m² ≈ 0.405 ha; 1 sq ft ≈ 0.0929 m²; 1,000 sq ft ≈ 93 m²; 1 mile ≈ 1.61 km.

**Practical example.** A 2,000 sq ft Florida house is about 186 m² — a large T4 in Portuguese terms.

**Examination implication.** Work in feet and acres. Front feet = the frontage dimension (the first number given).

**Memory aid.** Acre = 43,560 (think 43-5-60). Mile = 5,280 ('five tomatoes': 5-2-80).

**Practice question.** How many acres is a 435,600 sq ft parcel?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

10 acres (435,600 ÷ 43,560).

</details>

*Portuguese side: verified: arithmetic (1 ft = 0.3048 m exactly).* Lessons: L14-2, L10-2

## PT-18 · Mortgage affordability

**Portuguese context.** Banks apply a debt-service-to-income limit (taxa de esforço) on NET income under Banco de Portugal macroprudential measures. Your own Drive guide states the limit was lowered from 50% to 45% in May 2026; that figure requires verification.

**Florida context.** Exam convention: ratios use GROSS monthly income. Housing ratio = PITI ÷ gross income (conventional 28%); total ratio = (PITI + recurring debt) ÷ gross income (36%); FHA 31/43.

**The important difference.** Gross vs net income is the trap. PITI includes taxes and insurance.

**Practical example.** Gross $8,000/month, PITI $2,200, car $500: housing 27.5%, total 33.75% — qualifies conventionally.

**Examination implication.** Use gross income; include taxes and insurance in PITI.

**Memory aid.** Florida divides by GROSS.

**Practice question.** Which income figure do qualifying ratios use?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

Gross monthly income.

</details>

*Portuguese side: requires verification (user's guide_casa_portugal, June 2026).* Lessons: L12-3

## PT-19 · Foreclosure

**Portuguese context.** A lender enforces a mortgage (hipoteca) through court enforcement proceedings (execução). Requires verification.

**Florida context.** Florida foreclosure is judicial. The borrower may redeem by paying in full until the foreclosure sale (equity of redemption); there is no statutory right of redemption after the sale. Deficiency judgments are possible against personally liable parties.

**The important difference.** The exam tests the end point of redemption (the sale) and the deed-in-lieu trap (junior liens survive).

**Practical example.** A borrower offers full payment one day after the courthouse auction. Too late in Florida.

**Examination implication.** No post-sale redemption in Florida.

**Memory aid.** Redeem before the gavel.

**Practice question.** Does a deed in lieu of foreclosure wipe out a second mortgage?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

No. The lender takes title subject to junior liens; only foreclosure can eliminate them.

</details>

*Portuguese side: requires verification.* Lessons: L12-2

## PT-20 · Anti-discrimination in housing

**Portuguese context.** Portuguese law prohibits discrimination generally (constitutional equality and specific anti-discrimination legislation). Details require verification.

**Florida context.** The exam tests the US federal list: 1866 Civil Rights Act (race, no exceptions); Fair Housing Act (race, color, religion, national origin, sex, familial status, handicap); named practices (steering, blockbusting, redlining); exemptions and how they are lost. Florida's Fair Housing Act mirrors the federal one (details not verified in this session).

**The important difference.** US law uses a precise list of protected classes and named practices. Exam answers depend on exact categories and exemption conditions.

**Practical example.** Showing a buyer from Brazil only homes in 'neighbourhoods with Brazilian families' is steering on national origin, even if the buyer seems pleased.

**Examination implication.** No exemption ever for race.

**Memory aid.** Steer = guide buyers; block = scare sellers; red = lenders' map.

**Practice question.** A landlord with a 4-unit building who lives in one unit refuses to rent to a family with children and uses no broker or ads. Which exemption might apply?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

The 'Mrs. Murphy' owner-occupied (≤4 units) exemption under the federal FHA — but never for race, and lost if a broker or discriminatory ad is used.

</details>

*Portuguese side: requires verification.* Lessons: L07-1

## PT-21 · Advertising

**Portuguese context.** Mediation advertising is regulated (license identification in ads requires verification).

**Florida context.** Every advertisement must include the brokerage's registered name. An ad without it is a blind ad, in any medium, including social media. A sales associate's name must be as registered with DBPR; teams may not appear to be a separate brokerage.

**The important difference.** The required element is the BROKERAGE NAME (not a license number). Personal social-media ads by associates are included.

**Practical example.** An associate posts 'Just listed — DM me!' on Instagram with her own name only. Blind ad.

**Examination implication.** Owners advertising their own property need no brokerage name.

**Memory aid.** No firm name = blind ad.

**Practice question.** Does a sales associate's personal Facebook ad for a listing need the brokerage name?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

Yes.

</details>

*Portuguese side: requires verification.* Lessons: L05-3

## PT-22 · Residential leases

**Portuguese context.** Urban leases are governed by the Civil Code and the NRAU; written form and registration requirements require verification.

**Florida context.** A lease of 1 year or less may be oral; longer leases must be written (statute of frauds) but no longer need witnesses (s. 689.01, V-05). Notices to end tenancies without a specific term: 60/30/30/7 days. Deposit rules: 30-day notice of how held; 15/30/15 at move-out.

**The important difference.** Specific Florida day-counts are tested; Portuguese notice periods must not be transferred.

**Practical example.** A month-to-month tenant in Orlando must receive written notice at least 30 days before the end of a monthly period.

**Examination implication.** Use current s. 83.57 periods.

**Memory aid.** 60 / 30 / 30 / 7.

**Practice question.** How much notice ends a quarter-to-quarter tenancy without a specific term?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

At least 30 days before the end of the quarter.

</details>

*Portuguese side: requires verification.* Lessons: L07-4, L08-2

## PT-23 · Energy disclosures

**Portuguese context.** An energy certificate (certificado energético) is required to sell or rent; requires verification.

**Florida context.** Florida requires that buyers receive an energy-efficiency rating information brochure at or before contract — information, not a property rating.

**The important difference.** Florida's requirement is a brochure, not a rating of the specific property.

**Practical example.** The FR/BAR contract includes a clause acknowledging receipt of the energy brochure.

**Examination implication.** Required for sales of buildings for occupancy.

**Memory aid.** Florida: brochure, not certificate.

**Practice question.** Is a Florida seller required to obtain an energy rating of the home before listing?

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

No. The requirement is to provide the energy-efficiency information brochure to the buyer.

</details>

*Portuguese side: requires verification.* Lessons: L11-4
